lesson.title: Ordering Values: <, >, <=, and >=
lesson.summary: The ordering operators <, >, <=, and >= compare two values to decide which one comes first, letting programs express ranges, limits, and thresholds.
lesson.body:
Where == and != only ask whether two values match, the four ordering operators ask how values are arranged relative to each other. < evaluates to True when the left value is strictly smaller than the right value. > evaluates to True when the left value is strictly larger. <= and >= work the same way but also allow the two sides to be equal, which is why they read "less than or equal to" and "greater than or equal to." All four still produce a plain boolean result, True or False, following the same rules as every other comparison operator in this chapter.

These operators are not limited to numbers; Python can order strings as well, comparing them the way a dictionary would, character by character using each character's underlying code. "apple" < "banana" evaluates to True because "a" comes before "b" in that ordering. The fact that sorting a list of words alphabetically and comparing numbers by size both rely on the exact same set of operators underneath is not a coincidence; it is the same idea of ordering applied to different kinds of values.

The difference between the strict operators, < and >, and the inclusive ones, <= and >=, matters far more than it might seem, especially at boundaries. Consider a program that only allows entry to people 18 or older:

age = 18
can_enter = age >= 18
print(can_enter)

Because >= includes the case where the two sides are equal, age >= 18 evaluates to True when age is exactly 18. If the code had used age > 18 instead, someone who is precisely 18 would incorrectly be turned away, since 18 > 18 evaluates to False. Choosing the right operator for a boundary condition is a genuinely common source of bugs, sometimes called an off-by-one error.

These operators appear constantly in loop conditions as well. A loop written as while count < 10 stops the moment count reaches 10, running its body for the values 0 through 9, ten times total. Writing while count <= 10 instead would run the body an extra time, for count equal to 10 as well. Reading ordering operators carefully, and being deliberate about whether a boundary value should be included, is one of the most practical skills this section builds toward.

These operators also combine naturally with elif chains to build multi-way decisions, such as assigning a letter grade. A structure like if score >= 90: grade = "A" elif score >= 80: grade = "B" relies on evaluating each ordering comparison in sequence, stopping at the first one that evaluates to True. Because Python checks these conditions from top to bottom, the order they are written in matters just as much as the operators themselves; writing the score >= 80 check before the score >= 90 check would incorrectly grade a 95 as a B, since 95 >= 80 is also True and would be reached first, before the more specific and more accurate check ever runs.
